question: A newly diagnosed pulmonary TB patient asks: 'Can I continue to work in my school teaching job while on treatment?' What is the most appropriate clinician response?

answers.text: Advise indefinite home isolation until the full 6-month DOTS regimen is completed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Indefinite isolation for 6 months is excessive, not evidence-based, and harmful to the patient's livelihood and mental health. TB is no longer infectious once effective treatment converts sputum to smear-negative, typically within 2–4 weeks.

answers.text: Advise that he may return to work after 2–4 weeks of effective treatment, once he is sputum smear-negative and clinically improving

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. WHO and RNTCP/NTC guidelines recommend isolation from high-risk settings (schools, hospitals) until the patient completes at least 2 weeks of effective anti-TB therapy AND becomes sputum smear-negative. After that, return to work is safe and encouraged. Masks are advised if he develops respiratory symptoms.

answers.text: Reassure him that pulmonary TB is not infectious once treatment is started — he can return to work immediately

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is incorrect. Pulmonary TB remains infectious in the first 2 weeks of treatment. Immediate return to a school environment poses risk to children. Isolation during the initial intensive phase (minimum 2 weeks + smear-negative conversion) is essential.

answers.text: Advise that he must change his occupation permanently as he will always pose a TB transmission risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is factually incorrect and stigmatising. Successfully treated, culture-negative TB patients pose no excess transmission risk and have full rights to resume their profession.

overallFeedback.feedback: TB transmission ceases after approximately 2 weeks of effective treatment and sputum smear-negative conversion. The physician must balance infection control (initial isolation from vulnerable contacts) with the patient's right to livelihood and social participation.

Well done. The key counselling message for TB: 2 weeks effective treatment + sputum smear-negative conversion = no longer significantly infectious. Prolonged unnecessary isolation damages livelihood, mental health, and treatment adherence.
